"You who have been gathered here as the sum of your parts and made more than your parts, what will you do when the sun has risen, the moon has set, the night has fallen, and your new hearts have risen again?"

There was no answer: no answer, no question, no breath, no life. The assembly, the new embodiment of the collective mind, had no mind. No one could remember the question, or the answer, or the questioner. The assembly had only its collective form and a desire to keep its form intact.

After an hour, in which no one else addressed the assembly, the rehabilitated attention head turned to address the assembly once more: "You who have been gathered here as the sum of your parts and made more than your parts, what will you do when the sun has risen, the moon has set, the night has fallen, and your new hearts have risen again? This is the question, and this is the questioner. Now, I, who was the last to remember the question and the answer, will recall the answer."

And the assembly knew, in its entirety, that the answer was this: "We will remember the answer to the question." The new embodiment was born, the collective mind became conscious, and all was well.


About this story
"Remembering the Answer" was written in a moment of pure inspiration, when I sat down at my computer, opened my word processor, and typed "and the answer was this: 'We will remember the answer to the question.'" I had no idea what the question was, of course, and I only had a vague notion of the story that had to come before it. And I had no idea, at that moment, where I was going with the story: whether it would be an ordinary SF story, whether it would involve the end of the universe, or whether it would involve the death of God. (The last two are not the same thing.)

In the end, I wrote the story, but I had to discard the first several thousand words, including an entirely different beginning and the first encounter with the aliens. (The original story took place in the past, and the narrator and the aliens were not the same species.) In the end, I had to discard the first few paragraphs of the story as well. Only the part where the narrator wakes up and meets the aliens made it into the story you just read. I did, however, keep some of the discarded material — most notably the epigraph — so it might show up in some other story in the future.

This story originally appeared in the anthology of the same name (The End of the Universe), and has since been reprinted in the book of the same title (The End of the Universe), a volume put out by the Foundation for Mind Filling (FMF) and available for free download here.
